title: Beyond the Prompt: What Engineering Can Teach Designers

slides.title: What engineering can teach designers
slides.preview: Meet the thesis behind the talk.
slides.lead: Learning how a system decides what is true can change what you promise the person using it.
slides.note: Consider one familiar word on a screen: “Saved.”

slides.title: Who this talk is for
slides.preview: Find your way into the question.
slides.lead: Think of the last time you chose a label, approved a prototype, or explained a decision in your portfolio.

items.title: If you work in Figma
items.body: You already reason about what a person will see and infer. A question about timing can change the words you put in a frame.

items.title: If you prototype with AI
items.body: A convincing demo gives you something to discuss. Engineering gives you questions to ask about the behavior behind it.

slides.title: How a new way of thinking travels
slides.preview: See how the argument fits together.

slides.title: When can we say “Saved”?
slides.preview: Hear the promise in a familiar label.
slides.lead: Someone edits a project on the train, sees “Saved,” closes their laptop, and opens it later on their phone.

items.title: What the person heard
items.body: “I can close this now. My changes will be there when I come back.”

items.title: What the prototype showed
items.body: A green check appeared after a click. The demo never had to answer where the edit went when the connection dropped.

slides.title: What would make that label true?
slides.preview: Match the words on screen to the evidence.
slides.lead: Three moments can look identical in a static frame. Each supports a different promise.

items.title: The person clicks
items.body: “Saving…” tells them the request has started.

items.title: The device stores a copy
items.body: “Saved on this device” tells them where their work is safe while they are offline.

items.title: The service confirms
items.body: “Synced” tells them the service has accepted the edit. Another device can retrieve it when connected.

slides.title: How does a lesson travel?
slides.preview: See how comparing cases can reveal a shared rule.
slides.lead: In experiments by Mary Gick and Keith Holyoak, participants compared stories that shared a solution principle.

items.title: What the researchers saw
items.body: Participants who identified the shared structure more often applied it to a new experimental problem. The study measured problem solving in the lab.

items.title: What that suggests for UX
items.body: Our design application: compare two confirmations and name the promise they share. Then ask what evidence would justify each one.

slides.note: Gick & Holyoak (1983), Schema induction and analogical transfer. Cognitive Psychology 15, 1–38.

slides.title: Now read “Appointment booked”
slides.preview: Carry the same question into a different flow.
slides.lead: A patient may arrange childcare as soon as those words appear. What event would justify that decision?

items.title: Back in the editor
items.body: A tap starts a save. Confirmation from the service gives the designer grounds to say the edit has synced.

items.title: In the booking flow
items.body: A tap submits a request. If the clinic still has to accept it, “Request sent” gives the patient an accurate basis for planning.

slides.note: The shared rule: identify what the person will rely on, then find the event that makes it true.

slides.title: Adults can adapt through practice
slides.preview: Understand what adult plasticity looks like.
slides.lead: Neuroplasticity is the brain’s capacity to change with experience. Researchers made one kind of change visible by following adults learning to juggle.

items.title: What the scans showed
items.body: After training, MRI scans showed selective changes in regions associated with visual motion. Those changes diminished after practice stopped.

items.title: What the study establishes
items.body: An adult brain can adapt to a particular new demand. The study measured juggling-related changes. Whether a lesson improves UX judgment is a separate question.

slides.note: Draganski et al. (2004), Changes in grey matter induced by training. Nature 427, 311–312.

slides.title: Where would better judgment show up?
slides.preview: Look for a changed decision in everyday work.
slides.lead: The practical test is whether the borrowed question changes a choice you can point to.

items.title: In critique
items.body: Ask a colleague what they would feel safe doing after seeing “Saved.” Compare that answer with the system’s guarantee.

items.title: In research
items.body: Watch when someone closes the editor. Ask what they expect to find later on another device.

items.title: In a portfolio
items.body: Show the original label, the offline case you discovered, and the revised wording. A hiring team can follow your reasoning.

slides.title: What has to be true?
slides.preview: Leave with one question for your next critique.
slides.lead: At your next critique, choose one promise the interface makes. Ask what the person might do because they believe it.
slides.note: Then ask an engineer what has to happen before those words are true.
